content: The genus Salix includes willows, sallows, and osiers, comprising approximately 400 species of deciduous trees and shrubs. These plants are predominantly found in moist soils within cold and temperate regions of the Northern Hemisphere. While most species are commonly referred to as willows, certain narrow-leaved shrub species are called osiers, and some broader-leaved species are known as sallows. The term sallow is derived from the Latin word salix, meaning willow. Some willow species, particularly those adapted to arctic and alpine environments, grow as low-lying or creeping shrubs. For instance, the dwarf willow (Salix herbacea) rarely exceeds a height of 6 cm, yet it spreads extensively across the ground. Willows are highly cross-fertile, and numerous hybrids occur both naturally and through cultivation. A notable example is the weeping willow (Salix × sepulcralis), a widely planted ornamental tree that is a hybrid between the Chinese Peking willow and the European white willow. The leaves and bark of the willow tree have been recognized for their medicinal properties since ancient times. Historical texts from Assyria, Sumer, and Egypt document their use as remedies for aches and fever. The Greek physician Hippocrates also described their therapeutic benefits in the 5th century BCE. Native Americans across the American continent relied on willow as a cornerstone of their medical treatments due to its content of salicylic acid, a precursor to aspirin. In 1763, Reverend Edward Stone in England observed the medicinal properties of willow bark and reported his findings to the Royal Society, which subsequently published them. The active compound in willow bark, salicin, was isolated in crystalline form in 1828 by French pharmacist Henri Leroux and Italian chemist Raffaele Piria. Piria further succeeded in purifying the compound into its acid form, which was named salicylic acid. In 1897, Felix Hoffmann synthesized a chemically modified version of salicin, derived in his case from the Spiraea plant. This new compound caused less gastrointestinal irritation compared to pure salicylic acid. The resulting drug, formally known as acetylsalicylic acid, was named aspirin by Hoffmann's employer, Bayer AG. This innovation marked the beginning of the widely significant class of drugs known as non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs).
